      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/eisenkot-far-i-oppdrag-a-danne-regjering-i-israel-1.18076617</link>
      <description>Israels president har gitt opposisjonsleder Gadi Eisenkot i oppdrag å prøve danne regjering.
Hverken partiene som støtter statsminister Benjamin Netanyahu eller partiene som støtter Eisenkot fikk flertall ved valget 27. november.
Netanyahus blokk fikk 53 plasser i Knesset, mens blokken til Eisenkot fikk 48 mandater.
For å få flertall og bli statsminister trenger man 61 plasser i nasjonalforsamlingen. Begge blokkene er avhengig av de 19 mandatene fra de palestinsk-arabiske partiene, mend både Netanyahu og Eisenkot har sagt de ikke vil forhandle med dem.</description>

      <description>Casper Ruud har storspilt i Paris denne uken. Nå er han klar for semifinale etter seier over Nuno Borges.
Ruuds oppgjør mot portugiseren endte med 7-6 (7-5), 6-4. De to møttes for bare ni dager siden i Basel, og da snudde Borges kampen til seier.

      <description>Politiet opplyser at det har vært en front-mot-front-ulykke på E6 like ved Eidsvoll-tunnelen i sørgående løp.

Det satt en person i hver av bilene. En av dem er bekreftet død, den andre er kritisk skadet.

    <item>
      <title>NFF innfører semiautomatisert offside i Eliteserien</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/sport/nff-innforer-semiautomatisert-offside-i-eliteserien-1.18075445</link>
      <description>Det opplyser Fotballforbundet på en pressekonferanse fredag.
– Prisen har kommet ned til et nivå som gjør at muligheten er der, sier generalsekretær Karl-Petter Løken.
Han opplyser at innføringen vil skje i tråd med et dommerløft. NFF bevilger 5,5 millioner kroner i 2027 til dommerløftet, og 3,5 millioner av dem skal få til semiautomatisert offside.
NFF ønsker å øke dette til 7,5 millioner kroner i 2028, og gradvis trappe opp mot 2030.
– Det du har sett med disse linjene blir borte og du får disse visningene med menneskekropper hvor du ser helt tydelig at det er offside. Det er semiautomatisert offside. Det er det ene løftet, sier Løken og fortsetter:
– Det er en utgift som tas én gang og som vil følge oss, og så vil vi trappe opp resten av investeringen i dommerutviklingene i de andre tiltakene i tillegg. Så det blir en gradvis opptrapping, eksempelvis profesjonalisering. Vi starter stille og rolig og så blir det flere og flere.
Dette skjer etter et VAR-oppgjør blant flere toppklubber. Roenborg satt ned et eget utvalg som konkluderte med at «Dagens VAR fungerer for dårlig under norske forhold. De lovte forbedringene har ikke løst hovedutfordringene, og kostnadene er for høye i forhold til kvaliteten».
Utvalget til Rosenborg stilte seg også tvilende til at semiautomatisert offside ville hjelpe VAR i norsk fotball.
– Så det vil være penger ut av vinduet hvis tinget sier nei (til VAR)? spør NRK.
– Vi kommer ikke til å diskutere detaljer i den avtalen, svarer Klaveness.</description>

Det totale taket for elektriske utleiekjøretøy forblir på 16.000, men antallet elsparkesykler kuttes fra 16.000 til maksimalt 12.000. De resterende 4000 plassene settes av til elsykler når byrådet nå lyser ut ny anbudskonkurranse.
Byrådet setter også en fast nedre aldersgrense på 16 år for både elsykler og elsparkesykler.
– Vi hever aldersgrensen til 16 år sånn at vi styrker tryggheten både for dem som bruker elsykler- og elsparkesykler og for fotgjengere, sier Solberg.</description>

      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/boligprisene-falt-med-1-prosent-i-oktober-1.18073195</link>
      <description>Boligprisene i Norge falt med 1 prosent i oktober.
Det kommer frem i ferske tall fra Eiendom Norge. Sesongjustert steg prisene med 0,1 prosent.
– Det er normalt at boligprisene faller om høsten og i oktober i år var prisutviklingen svak i de fleste områdene i Norge, sier administrerende direktør Henning Lauridsen i Eiendom Norge i en pressemelding.
Hittil i år har prisene steget med 3,2 prosent. I september var dette tallet 4,2 prosent.
Gjennomsnittlig tid før en bolig blir solgt er 50 dager etter oktober, ifølge Eiendom Norge.
I oktober ble det solgt 8.970 boliger i Norge, noe som er 13,4 prosent færre enn i oktober 2025.
Til tross for nedgang i oktober, har Ålesund størst vekst i år, med 10,5 prosent.</description>

      <title>Abdul El-Sayed vinner i Michigan</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/abdul-el-sayed-vinner-i-michigan-1.18073068</link>
      <description>The New York Times erklærer at demokraten Abdul El-Sayed vinner over republikaneren Mike Rogers i kampen om sentatssetet i Michigan.
Det betyr at Demokratene går seirende ut av en av de mest profilerte valgene i dette mellomvalget.
Michigan var den eneste delstaten der Republikanerne hadde en realistisk mulighet til å ta et sete fra Demokratene i Senatet.
El-Sayed, som tilhører venstresiden i Det demokratiske partiet, blir den første senatoren som er muslim.
Sluttspurten i Michigan har vært preget av kontroverser. Haley Stevens, som tapte nominasjonskampen mot El-Sayed i høst, erklærte søndag sin støtte til republikaneren Rogers i stedet for partifellen El-Sayed.</description>

      <title>Én person til sykehus etter brann i Hamar</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/en-person-til-sykehus-etter-brann-i-hamar-1.18072929</link>
      <description>En firemannsbolig i Hamar er totalskadd etter en brann natt til onsdag.
13 personer blir nå ivaretatt på et hotell av kommunen, mens én person fortsatt er på sykehus, opplyser politiet i politiloggen.
Totalt er 14 personer rammet – åtte voksne og seks barn i alderen null til ni år. Brannvesenet jobber fremdeles med slukkearbeid på stedet, ifølge operasjonsleder Haagen Løvseth.</description>

“There’s a lot of work that needs to be done in Courtenay, Comox, Campbell River, and Qualicum Area,” Ted Olynyk told CHEK Saturday morning.

As of 1:30 p.m. Saturday, 3,463 households across Comox and Courtenay are still without power, according to BC Hydro’s outage list.

“It was quite a nasty event Friday; there were reports of a bomb basically dropping in the Courtenay-Comox area,” says Olynyk, adding “Extreme winds that caused lines and down branches.”

Friday evening, Comox Valley RCMP issued a traffic advisory warning drivers of a road closure, due to storm damage.

“Piercy Road between Greaves Crescent and Forbidden Plateau Road is closed due to falling trees and downed hydro lines. Please avoid the area and use an alternate route. Follow the direction of emergency personnel and allow extra time for travel,” stated Comox Valley RCMP’s online post.

“We had to ask people to stay off the roads so crews could do their work and not be on any lines,” says Olynyk.

Further up Island, a section of road near Qualicum remains closed due to a fallen tree.

DriveBC posted an update online Saturday that Highway 19 A “remains closed in both directions between Crane Rd and Horne Lake Rd due to trees on the road.”

Not to be mistaken for a violin, a talented viola player is celebrating joining the Victoria Symphony after a decade on the substitute list.

Jessica Pickersgill was born and raised in Victoria and started playing the violin when she was six. 

“They always wanted me to learn an instrument, so I think it was fun, but for longer than I care to admit, I did not enjoy it,” said Jessica with a laugh.

She switched to the viola in high school and started to think about her future.

“It was around Grade 11 when I realized, ‘Oh, I don’t know what else I’m good at, but I can do this.’ And the rest is history, as they say,” said Jessica.

She studied and played around the world, then returned home in 2016, where she started freelancing. 

Watch the story in the video below:

Loading the player...

Violinist Kathryn Weibe has been playing with Jessica for years.

“The way she plays her instrument, the way she performs with other people, the sound she makes, her musicality – but also she’s one of the most humble people I’ve ever met,” said Kathryn.

They are both passionate core members of the group Cascadia Strings. Their music and their close friendship are a perfect harmony.

“Making music is so intimate; to have that friendship alongside is just something I will always value and treasure,” said Kathryn.

It’s not easy being a professional musician, and Cascadia is just one of the jobs Jessica’s done to establish herself and make a living, including earning a spot on the sub list for the Victoria Symphony.

She’s been playing with the symphony on and off for 10 years. But she’s not a sub this season.

For the first time in 25 years, a permanent spot in the viola section opened up, and Jessica auditioned. 

“[It was] a very magical moment that I will not forget for the rest of my life,” she said.

It’s a unique and rare accomplishment that she’s extremely grateful for.

“It’s pretty magic. It’s an interesting thing because now my name’s in the program and I have a much more secure feeling, but it’s my home orchestra, and these are my colleagues and my friends,” she said.

“It’s nothing scary, it’s nothing intense, it’s more that this is where I’m meant to be.”

It says waterways are rising rapidly, with flows in parts of northern and western Vancouver Island reaching two- to five-year return levels on Friday.

High streamflow advisories cover most of the island as well as the south and central coasts, including the Sea to Sky region, and the lower Fraser River basin.

Environment Canada has meanwhile issued a coastal flooding statement for much of Vancouver Island’s west coast, saying elevated ocean levels combined with strong winds and waves could push waters above the highest astronomical tides.

“Crews are repairing damaged power lines, poles and other electrical equipment, with restoration work expected to continue throughout the day,” said BC Hydro in a release Saturday morning.

At the peak of Friday’s storm, about 80,000 customers were without power, but as the windstorm moved across B.C., the number of outages increased and outpaced crews’ ability to catch up.

“Friday’s storm caused significant damage, and we’re preparing for more challenging weather in the days ahead,” said Whitney Deane, BC Hydro spokesperson. “Additional weather systems are expected through mid-week, and some of the winds could be more impactful than what we’ve seen so far. Our crews and resources will be working around-the-clock to restore power and respond to new outages as quickly and safely as possible, and we’re encouraging customers to be prepared.”

Saturday morning, Environment Canada issued a wind warning for North Vancouver Island, saying damaging winds are expected to hit with gusts up to 110 km/h starting this morning.

“Another storm, currently located over the Eastern Pacific, is approaching the B.C. coast today. An associated frontal system will bring southeast winds gusting to 110 km/h to the region beginning this morning.”

Winds are expected to ease by late afternoon, but remain gusty overnight, it says.

“Local utility outages are possible. High-sided vehicles will be pushed around by the wind. Disruptions to services and travel are possible. Secure loose objects,” adds Environment Canada’s warning.

With more storms on the way, BC Hydro is warning customers to prepare for more outages.

“BC Hydro’s meteorologists are closely monitoring two, and likely three, more weather systems expected to impact the coast and other regions of the province between now and mid-week. The next system is expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds to the south and central coasts beginning Saturday, with some wind gusts potentially more damaging than those experienced so far.”

As for why the high number of outages Friday, BC Hydro’s new report suggests it could be connected to the extended season of drought and heat in B.C., leading to weakened trees and root systems that become more vulnerable in severe weather.

“Those effects can linger into fall and winter and may not become apparent until high winds and heavy rain put weakened trees under additional stress,” states BC Hydro.

In the past several years, BC Hydro has spent $150 million identifying and removing dangerous trees and vegetation near power lines, as part of it annual vegetation management spending.

As storm activity is expected to continue this weekend, BC Hydro says its extended storm response is in place with crews, contractors and other resources, including in-house meteorologists working 24/7 through the province.

Staying safe and prepared

“During an outage, customers should stay at least 10 metres away from downed, damaged or low-hanging power lines and call 911 to report them,” states BC Hydro.

By monitoring the weather systems, their teams are ready to respond to the anticipated high-risk areas.

BC Hydro advises households to keep a stocked 72-hour emergency kit with water, non-perishable food, flashlights, batteries, and first-aid supplies.

Download the BC Hydro mobile app, which provides outage information specific to a customer’s address, including the cause, when the outage began, the estimated restoration time, and the latest updates. You can also learn more about staying prepared – and the latest outages – at bchydro.com.

]]> 1359917 Food Bank on the Edge expands reach as more ‘working families’ access the service https://cheknews.ca/food-bank-on-the-edge-expands-reach-as-more-working-families-access-the-service-1359707/ Sat, 07 Nov 2026 15:00:00 +0000 https://cheknews.ca/?p=1359707

Ucluelet, B.C. – Budgets are stretched thin and food banks across Canada are seeing more people with full-time jobs accessing their services.

Food Banks Canada’s annual HungerCount project tracks and reports on food bank visits and client demographics. This year, the non-profit said food bank usage has nearly doubled since March 2019, and nearly 18 per cent of food bank clients reported having a job, compared to 12 per cent in 2019.

Food Bank on the Edge serves the west coast communities of Ucluelet, Tofino, Millstream, Port Albion, Hitacu, Opitsaht, Ty-Histanis/Esowista, Ahousaht, Hesquiaht and Toquaht. It is accredited under Food Banks Canada’s Standards of Excellence program, which sets the benchmark for safety, dignity and operational excellence in food banking. 

Last September 2025, the non-profit moved into a new facility at 362 Forbes Road in Ucluelet, moving the region’s food security hub up from a musty, low-lying space at the Seaplane base parking lot to high ground.  

Over a cup of cinnamon spice tea, long-standing volunteer Cris Martin says it’s “shocking” how many more “working families” they are seeing come in. 

“But that’s the reality,” said Martin. “You don’t know what people are coming to you with; it could be debt or medical expenses… (The food bank) is not a shameful place to come. There was always that cloud, especially with men. It doesn’t have to be that way. We are here to help and support,” she offered.

Rising costs have impacted the Food Bank on the Edge’s regular list of hamper items as well. The non-profit recently nixed coffee from their distribution list to save money. 

“We did the math and a portion of coffee, which is usually about one pound, cost almost as much as hamburger meat,” said Martin, adding they don’t buy cheese anymore either. 

Food Bank on the Edge is expanding operations to keep up with the “new normal”, according to Executive Director Carla Davis. She says Christmas hampers will be delivered throughout the west coast this year, and she put a call out to volunteers in the Tofino area.

“It’s going to be a huge undertaking. We will need a volunteer base in Tofino,” said Davis, who started the part-time role in September. 

In the past, Christmas hampers were only given out to families living south of the Tofino-Ucluelet junction.

Serving remote communities

Unlike larger urban centres with several grocery stores to lean on, Food Bank on the Edge only collects from one grocery store, the Ucluelet Co-op. They also regularly deliver hampers directly to families within their area of service through a contract held by the Westcoast Community Resources Society (WCRS). 

“We are servicing so many remote communities and our outreach workers that do the deliveries need more funding,” Davis said.

Ucluelet First Nation sends a delegate each month to pick up hampers for their members living in Hitacu, a role Davis said has helped with the “balancing act” of taking care of so many remote communities. 

With just under 50 per cent of Food Bank on the Edge’s clients living in Nuu-chah-nulth communities, Davis says she would love to establish a monthly delivery contact with Tla-o-qui-aht, Ahousaht, Toquaht and Hesquiaht as well to streamline transportation costs.

“It’s difficult for people to get here,” she said. 

Tla-o-qui-aht member Maria Clark is the Assistant General Manager at Tofino’s Tin Wis Resort, a Tla-o-qui-aht First Nations owned and operated accommodation provider. 

Clark shared that Tin Wis recently conducted a labour market research study to learn what barriers Tla-o-qui-aht community members face when it comes to participating in the workforce. 

“Being able to feed my family, today” was listed as the main priority for many respondents, according to Clark. 

“Realistically, what we are considering living wages right now are still only getting some people paycheque to paycheque. It doesn’t include what the actual cost of daycare can be if your child isn’t in the $10-a-day program,” said Clark.

“Is it cheaper to stay home and not work and not pay daycare?” Clark continued.

In 2024, the living wage for a family of four in the Clayoquot Biosphere Region was $27.40, according to the Clayoquot Biosphere Trust. The living wage is based on expenses faced by two parents working 35 hours a week and two children under 10. It does not capture unique transportation expenses faced by families that rely on water taxis or personal boats for everyday activities.

Food Bank on the Edge clients peaked in 2020 during the pandemic with 3,296 people served. In 2024, the non-profit served 2,257 people and spent about $40,800 on groceries. In 2025 it served 2,093 clients and spent just under $45,000 on groceries. So far, 2026 has seen 1,549 people visit the food bank, but with November and December being the busiest time for the west coast food bank, Davis says the numbers will likely look the same as last year. 

Partnership with Tofino Ucluelet Culinary Guild 

Tofino Ucluelet Culinary Guild (TUCG) is helping with logistics, people power and sourcing products when it comes to collecting donations for the Christmas hamper expansion this year. TUCG is a collective that connects restauranteurs and community members to locally sourced ingredients.

“We want to help them reach more people,” said TUCG Executive Director Rob Renna.  

He reflected on the rising cost of goods with a long sigh. From the price of diesel to packaging, he says everywhere they look, things are getting more expensive.  

“Affordability is certainly a growing challenge. As a non-profit, we work hard to keep our operating costs as low as possible, while also recognizing the pressures facing local farmers and producers who are dealing with rising costs of their own. We’re seeing people become more cautious with their spending. The reality is that the rising cost of living is making things increasingly difficult for everyone on the coast, from farmers and food producers to local families,” said Renna.

“We are at the will of the world market that’s why, for us, we are really proud of supporting the small farmer on Vancouver Island and being able to get the products to chefs and individuals here,” he continued.

Davis encouraged anyone to reach out if they need a hamper, to make a donation or to volunteer: 250-726-6909 or foodbankedge@gmail.com.

Instead of completing the job, he said DFO left a migratory barrier at the site – and a lot of unanswered questions.

“How could they leave this stream to die on the operating table? What was the showstopper? I’d like to know,” Hurwitz cussed. 

A couple years ago on October 19, 2024, Hurwitz said a “catastrophic” rainfall event caused the fish ladder to fail at Salmon Creek, a spot in Yuułuʔiłʔatḥ territory known as Glukamukus Creek. Thornton Creek staff made urgent repairs to the ladder system that same week, and plans were initiated with DFO to replace the aging infrastructure.  

Summer 2025 came and went, and Hurwitz says DFO “couldn’t do anything” about Salmon Creek that year due to capacity limitations. Then summer 2026 arrived and DFO showed up with a crew at Salmon Creek to build a new fish ladder that would assist the fish in accessing a culvert that leads to their spawning grounds. 

“Before the road went in you didn’t need a culvert. The river just flowed. Once we built the road, we needed a culvert so the fish can get up. Once we build something we have to take care of it,” he said.

On Sept. 11, Hurwitz said he went to check on the site and saw DFO shutting the project down. 

“I don’t know who stuck a fork in it,” said Hurwitz. “I don’t really know why they stopped. They still had a couple days in the fisheries window. There was no rain coming for a few days and they were right there. Like, why didn’t they get it done?”

The site was left in such a state that the chum salmon would need to make a three- to four-foot jump to access the culvert. 

James Costello, Thornton Creek Hatchery operation manager, says there’s no way a chum can jump that high. 

“Chum are poor jumpers. Anything over about a foot or two they are not going to be able to get up. They are very strong, but they are terrible jumpers,” said Costello.

Silver lining 

The silver lining to this story is the crew of volunteers that came together to move thousands of fish up into the culvert by hand. It’s been a team effort with folks from Toquaht Nation, Ucluelet First Nation, Redd Fish Restoration and other friends showing up to help, Hurwitz said.

“It speaks to people working together to help make the world better,” said Hurwitz. “It’s been a ton of work, but it’s turned into a great community initiative. People have rallied around this. It’s been a great opportunity for us to show gentle fish handling.”

Costello says it’s “unfortunate” that the timing of the abandoned ladder project lined up with a strong chum return; he says there’s been over 3,000 fish in the run this year. 

Without the assistance from volunteers, Costello says the chum would have only been able to use three quarters of the creek system, and the fish would have “timed out downstream”, dumping their eggs or dying with their eggs inside them.

“We are so happy to have the assistance from the community. It’s a lot of manual labour. It’s a labour of love,” Costello notes.

Ucluelet-based marine biologist Dane Stabel spent a couple days volunteering at Salmon Creek. Alongside 15 or so others, Stabel netted salmon and then dropped them by hand into a pipe that flowed into the culvert. They also gathered a subset of brood stock for the Thornton Creek Hatchery’s spawning program. 

“It’s beautiful that there are so many people that care about fish and salmon. Sometimes the charismatic mammals get all the attention, but I find salmon are a good ambassador for fish,” said Stabel. 

“(Salmon) are very important to the ecosystem and the culture here. It pretty much feeds everything. They are incredibly interesting. It’s hard not to root for an animal that goes through such a crazy journey just to spawn. There are very few animals who work as hard as these guys to get the next generation going,” he said.

DFO said that the installation of the concrete fish ladder, or rock weirs, could not be completed at the time “due to unsafe work conditions”. 

“The second and final phase of construction is scheduled for the late summer 2027 fisheries timing window, and the rock weirs will be installed,” said DFO in a written statement to the Ha-Shilth-Sa News.

“Once completed, the rock weirs will improve fish passage and support salmon migration under natural watershed conditions, provided sufficient flow is available within the system,” they said.

Hurwitz is shaking his head in disbelief. He hopes something like this never happens again. 

“When you’re dealing with live animals, you can’t make mistakes. You can’t screw it up. It’s not carpentry. If we screw something up, we are robbing Mother Nature,” he said.

As of Nov. 2, Hurwitz says the volunteer team has moved 2,587 chum salmon through the culvert up to their spawning grounds.
